UX Case Study  ·  Amplicomm  ·  Omnichannel Analytics

Turning a generic BI tool into a product sellers actually trust.

Amplicomm's analytics dashboard started as a lightly customized Superset instance. I led the redesign that turned it into a focused product for e-commerce sellers tracking performance across every channel they sell on.

01

Context & the problem

Assumption — confirm with me

Amplicomm gives e-commerce sellers one place to see performance across every channel they sell on — Amazon, Flipkart, and others — instead of checking each marketplace's own dashboard separately.

  • The product I inherited was a customized Apache Superset instance — powerful underneath, but visually and structurally still a generic BI tool.
  • Sellers didn't have one obvious place to look when they opened it, and the KPIs that actually mattered to their business were buried among charts that didn't.
  • My read: this was a trust and clarity problem as much as a visual one — a seller needs to trust a number before they'll act on it, and a screen with five equally-loud charts doesn't build that trust.
Where I'm filling gaps with judgment

I don't yet have your original problem brief, so this framing is my read of the evidence you shared (the heuristic critique and the redesigned spec). Tell me if the actual business driver was different — e.g. a specific churn number, a sales pitch to new sellers, or a technical migration deadline — and I'll rewrite this section around the real reason.

02

Starting with an honest audit

Your original artifact

Before proposing anything new, I ran a structured heuristic evaluation of the existing dashboard — the kind of unglamorous first step that's easy to skip and expensive to skip badly.

  • Too many distractions competing for attention on one screen.
  • No focal point — the eye had nowhere obvious to land first.
  • KPIs that mattered most weren't visually prioritized over anything else.
  • "Month to Date" and "Year to Date" labels weren't self-explanatory to a non-analyst seller.
  • Redundant elements (duplicate axis labels already shown elsewhere) added noise without adding information.
  • No consistent visual language across the screen.
Why start here

An audit like this turns "I don't like how this looks" into a numbered list stakeholders can actually evaluate and prioritize against — which is what let a CEO, CTO, and CPO agree on scope quickly instead of relitigating taste.

03

Four principles, applied everywhere

Rather than redesign screen by screen, I set four principles up front so every dashboard — not just the home screen — would answer the same audit consistently.

04

The redesigned Home dashboard

Your original artifact

The spec below isn't just a visual redesign — every interaction is documented as a rule, which is what let two junior designers extend the pattern to other dashboards consistently without me reviewing every screen personally.

And here's the same dashboard, shipped — empty state next to four KPIs actively compared.

Why the empty state matters

The dashboard defaults to one metric, one line, one color — the "no focal point" problem literally cannot recur here. Complexity is something the seller opts into, one checkbox at a time, not something they're handed on load.

Selected period panel

Quick tabs (1D/1W/1M/6M/1Y) plus a calendar picker. Selecting a period always shows the resulting date range back to the user in plain text — directly answering "MTD/YTD isn't self-explanatory."

KPI panel drives the chart

Selecting a KPI changes which line renders below it and assigns it a consistent color. Hovering a compared period shows a dotted line instead of committing to it — a low-cost way to preview a comparison before locking it in.

Compare metrics panel

Sellers can check multiple KPIs to overlay as separate lines, each with a distinct stroke color reflected in the legend — letting them ask "how did GMV move against orders?" without leaving the chart.

Consistent dropdown language

Chart-type, item-quantity, and label (Value/Variance) controls share the same interaction pattern everywhere they appear — a small thing that's exactly what "screen lacks consistency" was calling out.

05

Cross-filtering for multiple personas

Assumption — confirm personas & details

The top filter bar (Tenant, Channel, Category, SKU, Brand) covered the obvious case, but different roles inside the same seller organization were asking fundamentally different questions of the same data — and rebuilding those filters manually every time was slow for all of them.

  • Made any chart element — a channel slice, a category bar, a low-stock insight — clickable as a live filter, instantly re-filtering every other chart and KPI on the dashboard.
  • The resulting selection appears as a real, removable filter chip in the top bar, so the state stays visible and shareable rather than hidden inside a click history.
  • One interaction model, reused everywhere, meant a founder, a category manager, an ads lead, and an operations lead could each get to their own answer without four separate dashboards to maintain.
Where I'm filling gaps with judgment

You gave me the feature name and its multi-persona intent; I inferred the specific personas (founder, category manager, marketing lead, operations lead) and their example use cases from what's plausible for an omnichannel seller analytics tool, and from the KPIs already visible in your Home dashboard (TACOS, SKU Availability, Delivery Lead Time). Tell me the real personas and I'll replace these with the actual ones and their actual triggers.

06

Leading through the work

This wasn't a design team working in isolation and presenting finished screens — every major decision was made in the room with the people who'd have to live with its consequences.

  • Led two junior designers — my job was to keep every dashboard answering the same four principles, not just the Home screen I personally designed.
  • Worked with the CTO directly on what Superset's underlying query engine could realistically support, so designs didn't promise interactions engineering couldn't ship on the existing data stack.
  • Worked with the CEO and CPO to keep scope tied to business priorities — this was a startup, and every week of design time had a visible opportunity cost.
  • Partnered with PM on sequencing which dashboards got redesigned first, based on which ones sellers actually opened most.

08

Reflection

Draft — confirm or replace

What I'd want to add

Real usage data on which KPIs sellers actually compare most, to check whether the compare-metrics panel's default state matches real behavior.

A constraint worth naming

Building on top of Superset meant some ideal interactions were bounded by what the underlying query engine could do fast enough for a seller who wants an instant answer.

What I'd revisit

Whether "depth on demand" (maximise view, compare panels tucked behind clicks) is undiscoverable for less analytically confident sellers — worth a usability pass focused on first-time use.

What held up well

Documenting interactions as explicit rules, not just static screens, is what let two junior designers apply the system consistently without constant review.
